title: InferLens
headline: Making LLM inference legible.
summary: A browser tool that opens a recorded vLLM trace and shows where the time went (queue, prefill, decode), with metrics, an animated replay, charts, and a beginner walkthrough.

demo.alt: InferLens home page showing one request split into queue, prefill, and decode
demo.caption: The InferLens home page: one recorded Qwen3-4B request on vLLM, split into queue (5 ms), prefill (79 ms), and decode (1,766 ms).

sections.heading: The problem
sections.body: When an LLM answers slowly, it's hard for newcomers to tell why. A single reply is made of waiting in a queue, reading the prompt (prefill), and writing tokens one at a time (decode), and raw numbers like TTFT and TPOT don't show which stage the time went to.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.body: InferLens opens a trace file recorded from a vLLM run and turns it into something you can see. It shows the run configuration, latency and throughput metrics, GPU and KV-cache utilization, and an animated replay of the run. Charts cover queue dynamics, KV-cache use over time, phase durations, and token cadence. Everything runs in the browser; the trace never leaves your computer.

sections.heading: Learning the pipeline
sections.body: A separate Learn page walks a beginner through one ordinary 1.85-second reply, step by step: the wait, the read, and the long stretch of writing. Each step shows how the formulas for TTFT, TPOT, and throughput come straight from that trace.

sections.heading: How it's built
sections.body: InferLens is split across three teams: inference collects measurements from vLLM, analysis owns the shared trace schema and derived metrics, and the frontend loads that trace. I built the frontend: trace loading, metric cards, the queue, prefill, and decode timelines, the dashboard charts, the animation and styling, and the first version of the Learn page. It's framework-free JavaScript, every chart is hand-drawn SVG, and it's covered by Node tests.

title: One Minute Utopia
headline: A clearer path to Baltimore 311.
summary: Snap a photo of a broken streetlight or cracked road and you're done: Gemini classifies it, similar reports are grouped into one incident, and an agent files it with the right city agency once it matters.

demo.caption: Hop Hacks 2026 – One Minute Utopia. Try the live app with the Live demo button above.

sections.heading: The problem
sections.body: Apps like Citizen surface gunshots and fires, but almost nobody reports a cracked road or a broken traffic light, and many people don't know 311 handles them. Reporting through agency websites or a 311 call is slow (one of us waited about 10 minutes on hold), and research shows people report less when the process is longer. Small problems go unfixed because reporting them is a chore.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.body: You take a picture. Gemini classifies the issue and the app attaches time and location automatically. That's all the user does, and it takes seconds. Behind the scenes, reports in the same category with overlapping locations are merged into a single incident, and each report gets a severity score from 1 to 10 (litter is around 4, a badly cracked road around 7). Serious issues are escalated right away; minor ones wait until enough people report them, so the city only hears about problems that actually bother people, and never gets duplicates.

sections.heading: Beacon, the reporting agent
sections.body: Once an incident's score is high enough, Beacon works out which agency should get it, fills in that agency's web form with Playwright, and flags the incident as reported so it's never filed twice. To avoid sending test data to real agencies, Beacon runs against two mock government sites we built. In the meantime, users are shown the right contact info and form links for their issue.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.body: Three parts: a Next.js front end, a Node.js and Supabase (SQL) backend, and the Playwright reporting agent, with the Gemini API for image analysis, Leaflet and OpenStreetMap for the incident map, and Vercel for hosting. We developed with an agentic workflow: four coding agents with separate roles for development, review, QA, and polish.

sections.heading: What we learned
sections.body: It was our first hackathon, and we shipped a working full-stack app that does everything we set out to do. The hard parts were setting up the Gemini API on Google Cloud, building reliable image analysis, and finding a consistent rule for when an incident deserves to be reported. Next: real government reporting APIs, cities beyond Baltimore, and stronger validation of AI confidence and user trust.
